questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Improving my Spanish speaking abilities and visiting and exploring a country and a culture that was previously quite unfamiliar to me. I chose Mexico partly because it is one of the countries where i had the easiest time understanding the Spanish spoken there, and because what i had seen of Mexican culture before going seemed very interesting to me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The people at the school were very helpful, but i did often have to go to the different faculties, which takes a lot of time since Mexico City is so large that taking a 1,5 to 2 hour trip just to sign some papers or getting some basic information seems excessive, additionally the information provided by UNAM is generally only in Spanish, which was fine but it would have been nice to get in English as well so could be sure that i didn't misunderstand anything due to lacking Spanish skills

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I met with the administrator of the carrera who helped me get an overview of the provided classes, and was also put into contact with another student from the carrera through their Unamigo program which was very helpful with questions that weren't centered on practical school information

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used a service called Internship in Mexico, who put me in contact with the owner of an apartment in Mexico City, the apartment was not great, partly because it is mostly exchange students living there for 1-2 semester so they tend not to care as much or take as good care of the apartment as they would somewhere more permanent. It was nice to live with other exchange students, since they can more easily understand the things that may be hard while studying very far away from home that your mexican classmates might not relate to

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: May depend on where you live, but talking to other foreign exchange students, it seems like landlords don't put in a lot of work to fix things in the apartment, especially when it is mostly exchange students living there, since the landlord knows they'll leave soon.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UNAM provides no housing for regular or exchange students, and it is quite hard to find a good place before arriving since you can't see it in person and pictures might be misleading

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very easy to register for courses, but not a wide variety of different courses within the carrera because they only do summer starts, if you go in the spring you can only choose classes from 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th semester, and they have pretty set classes with many of them being continuations of a previous class. It doesn't make a lot of sense to take English IV and English VI at the same time since they are pretty much the same, one is just at a higher level.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I went to the faculty and talked to the administrator of the carrera and told her which classes i was thinking of taking, and got a short introduction to them, then i had to come back two days later to get sign the registration.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: In terms of registration there wasn't a lot of help besides the people who worked at the school, but i didn't feel like i needed much more than that.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes i wanted, i don't think the classes they offer really change from semester to semester, they have some electoral classes that might, but i couldn't sign up for those.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: At least at the carrera i studied at, the syllabus is not really used in the actual classes or teaching, so don't make your decision based on the syllabus, but look at a description of the class and what the goals of the class is instead

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses at my carrera were very low, the carrera is called English Teaching, and i knew that the level of english is generally lower in Mexico compared to Denmark, but the classes were closer to highschool level than university in my opinion. In most classes no readings are assigned for the entire semester, and when teachers did assign readings nobody did them, and then the following classes were spent explaining and summarizing what was in the readings instead of actually working with the materials

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is much more focused on classroom teaching, there is a 80% mandatory attendance, and they generally don't assign readings, they might assign homework for a class, but generally the homework is done fairly quickly and easily. The teaching is more focused on practical aspects, which makes sense since it is English teaching and not just English, as in Denmark, they did not work with theory in any of the subjects, but did a lot of group work and stuff like it in the classroom.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: English VI, Investigation into Applied Linguistics, Literature in English II, Psycholinguistics, Translation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The only course i took that i would recommend is translation, I don't feel that i learned much about translation since we the class didn't include any theory and i have already done two semesters of translation before going, but it was a really good way to improve my Spanish, if you are already fluent in Spanish and English, you may not get that much out of it.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Most of the unexpected costs were related to renting out my apartment in Denmark while abroad, other than that i don't think there was much, if there were it was not an large amount

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of imported items in supermarkets, either from Europe or the US, these are very expensive, fx. you can get mexican brand pasta for about 7-10 dkk but if you get the imported pasta it will cost about 50dkk, and sometimes the labels are not great in the supermarkets. Other than that, wine is very expensive compared to europe and tequila is very cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were sports teams and equipment available, additionally there was a language center where you can take language classes, and do other cultural activities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you need help with Spanish, or another language, university language classes are a good way to improve while building a social circle at university, and they are usually free or very cheap for students. Outside of school, i think the best is dance, usually in mexico salsa and bachata classes, there are a lot of different people, both young and older.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Coyoacan is a very nice part of town with a lot of markets where you can buy local food specialties, souvenirs, and other things, Puebla takes one or two hours to get to but is very nice to stay at for one or two nights. Chapultepec and the castle which is near the anthropological museum, which is nice, but very large so i don't recommend trying to see it all in one go, especially since UNAM students get into almost all museums free.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: A little difficult, though i think it was more due being so far away from friends and family and suddenly losing all routines i had in my life, it helps that people are very talkative here, and since there wasn't many exchange students at my faculty people are very eager to talk to someone not from mexico and hear why they chose to come here.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: People will likely invite you to a lot of things, especially in the beginning when you are getting adjusted to everything and are more tired than usual, they tend to understand if you explain why you can't/dont want to go, but try to say yes sometimes even if you dont have a lot of energy, since doing since outside of the school framework helps you getting friends faster

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Compared to in Denmark it feels like it is more important what you say than what you do, especially with being polite, It is very important to greet people and saying thank you and please and goodbye, but unlike in Denmark, it is not really considered rude to be late, or to invite someone to something and then cancel last minute, which can be frustrating if you aren't expecting it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and helpfulness, sometimes when asking people for help i would feel bad because they would go so far out of their way to help me that i felt i was impeding what they had to do, but i think the culture is just more helpful in general.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- If you are unsure of anything or need help, talk to your teacher, they are a lot closer to the students than in Denmark since they have more classes and will likely be very accommodating to whatever you might need, especially when you are on exchange.
- join a whatsapp group for exchange students, i was in two called CDMX, events parties and trips & Exchange CDMX, its a good way to meet other exchange students and go on trips outside the city that you might not feel comfortable doing alone.
- The culture at mexican universities is very different from danish universities, it is seen as a bit weird to be alone on campus and people might approach you and ask you about it if you walk around, eat, read alone on campus, but they mean it in a friendly way, usually.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Go visit the other faculties, especially Ciudad Universitaria has a lot of fun things, like small shops and museums

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting outside of my comfort zone, improving my spanish speaking abilities very rapidly, and meeting some of my roommates who were also on exchange.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting used to the daily life, stuff like stuff not working properly in my apartment, having to spend more than 3 hours every day going back and forth from university to my apartment.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
